*Iron screw, bolt, or nail (other metals won't work)

added: {{fa}}In an electromagnet, an electric current runs through a piece of metal and creates a magnetic field. To create a simple electromagnet, you'll need a source of electricity, a conductor, and metal. Wrap insulated copper wire tightly around an iron screw or nail before connecting the wire to a battery, and watch as your new electromagnet picks up small metal objects. Remember that you're creating electricity, so be careful when working with the electromagnet to ensure you don't hurt yourself.

#*You can use the small piece of iron for this, such as a nail, screw, or bolt.

added: In an electromagnet, an electric current runs through a piece of metal and creates a magnetic field. To create a simple electromagnet, you'll need a source of electricity, a conductor, and metal. Wrap insulated copper wire tightly around an iron screw or nail before connecting the wire to a battery, and watch as your new electromagnet picks up small metal objects. Remember that you're creating electricity, so be careful when working with the electromagnet to ensure you don't hurt yourself.

#Create a loose strand of copper wire. Use a spool of insulated copper wire to wrap around the iron core. Before you start wrapping the wire, leave a strand of wire loose from the iron that will attach to the battery. The loose end should be about {{convert|2-3|in|cm}} long.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX9QBwJBI_Y#t=25s</ref>

#Wrap insulated copper wire around the iron going in one direction. You want to create an ongoing spiral around the piece of iron. #Push the wire close together as you’re wrapping it. The wire should be wrapped tightly around the iron, and you want as many spirals as possible to create the best current. As you’re wrapping, use your fingers to push the loops close together. Continue wrapping and pushing the wire until you get to the end of the iron.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XKUs7Dc9pKI#t=25s</ref>
#*The more wire you use, the stronger the electrical current, so be careful and use caution when creating your magnet.
#*There is no certain number of wraps that you need, but the entire piece of iron should be covered in wire, with the strands of wire pushed right up against each other.

#Cut the wire so that the end is roughly {{convert|2-3|in|cm}} long. Once you reach the opposite end of the iron core, use wire cutters or sharp scissors to cut off the wire from the rest of the spindle. The second end should be as long as the first so that the wire tips can reach the battery equally.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX9QBwJBI_Y#t=53s</ref>
#*As you remove the insulation, the wire should turn from the copper color of the insulation to the natural silver color of the wire.

#Curl the ends of the wire to create a small circle. Use your fingers to bend the ends of the wire into a very small circle, about {{convert|0.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter. These circles will touch the center of each end of the battery.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX9QBwJBI_Y#t=55s</ref>

#Test out the magnet while holding the wire onto ends of the battery. Once you have a good grip on the battery with the wires, test it out! Hold the battery and iron close to a small metal object, such as a paperclip or safety pin. If the nail, screw, or bolt picks up the metal object, the magnet is working.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX9QBwJBI_Y#t=1m20s</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 6.jpg|center]]

#Use a power pack instead of a single battery for more power. Power packs last longer and create a stronger electric current than a single battery. #*Do a little research before picking out a larger battery pack to be sure you're picking one that's safe and will work.
#*The wire ends should go where the positive and negative terminals are.

#Find a larger piece of metal to create a stronger magnetic field. Instead of using a nail, try using a metal rod that's about {{convert|1|ft|cm|abbr=on}} long. Be sure to use it with a power pack to create a stronger magnet. It'll take a lot more copper wire to go around the entire piece of metal, so make sure you start with a full spindle.<ref>https://sciencing.com/make-super-strong-permanent-magnets-6520830.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 14.jpg|center]]
#*If you're using a larger piece of metal, it's only necessary to wrap the strand of metal with one layer of wire for safety reasons.

#Add more wraps of wire to form a stronger magnet. The more coils you create, the stronger the electric current. Get a large spindle of wire and make as many wraps as you can around an iron nail or screw to create a very powerful magnet, adding several layers of wire on top of one another, if desired.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 15.jpg|center]]
#*You can use the small piece of iron for this, such as a nail, screw, or bolt.
#*Wrap the wire in a single direction going around the piece of iron.
*Battery power pack (optional)
*Larger piece of metal (optional)

added: To make an electromagnet, an electric current is run through a piece of metal, which creates a magnetic field. To create a simple electromagnet, you'll need a source of electricity, a conductor, and metal. Wrap insulated copper wire tightly around an iron screw or nail before connecting the wire to a battery, and watch as your new electromagnet picks up small metal objects.
===Wrapping the Iron with Wire===

#Choose an iron nail or screw as the core. Pick out a piece of iron that you have around your home, such as a nail, screw, or bolt. It should be about {{convert|3-6|in|cm}} in length so that there’s plenty of room to wrap the wire around the iron object.<ref>https://education.jlab.org/qa/electromagnet.html</ref>

#Position copper wire so that there’s a strand loose next to the iron. Use a spool of insulated copper wire to wrap around the iron core. Before you start wrapping the wire, leave a strand of wire loose from the iron that will attach to the battery. The loose end should be about {{convert|2-3|in|cm}} long.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX9QBwJBI_Y</ref>
#*Position the wire so that it’s perpendicular to the iron core and at one end.

#Wrap insulated copper wire around the iron tightly. Start at an end of the iron and begin wrapping the copper around the iron in a tight spiral. Wrap the wire in one continuous strand, going in one direction, so that there’s a strong electrical current.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX9QBwJBI_Y</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 4.jpg|center]]
#*The tighter the spiral the better—the wire should be firmly pressed against the iron.

#*It's essential that the wire is wrapped in the same direction so the electricity flows in one direction. If you wrap the wire in different directions, the electricity will flow in different directions, and you won't create a magnetic field.

#Push the wire close together as you’re wrapping it. While the wire should be wrapped tightly around the iron, you also want as many spirals as possible to create the best current. As you’re wrapping, use your fingers to push the loops close together. Continue wrapping the wire until you get to the end of the iron.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XKUs7Dc9pKI</ref>
#*If you’re using a super thin wire and want a really strong current, you can wrap additional layers over the first layer of wire once you reach the end of the bolt.
===Creating Conductible Ends===

#Cut the wire so that the end is roughly {{convert|2-3|in|cm}} long. Once you reach the opposite end of the iron core, use wire cutters or sharp scissors to cut off the wire from the rest of the spindle. The second end should be as long as the first so that the wire tips can reach the battery equally.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX9QBwJBI_Y</ref>

#Remove {{convert|1-2|cm|in|abbr=on}} of insulation from the ends of the wires. You can use wire strippers, sandpaper, or a razor to carefully scrape off the insulation from each end. This will help the wires conduct energy more easily.<ref>https://education.jlab.org/qa/electromagnet.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 2.jpg|center]]
#*As you remove the insulation, the wire should turn from the copper color to a silver.

#Curl the ends of the wire to create a small circle. Use your fingers to bend the ends of the wire into a very small circle, about {{convert|0.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter. These circles will touch the center of each end of the battery.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX9QBwJBI_Y</ref>
#*Curling the ends of the wires helps the battery maintain good contact with the wire.

#Position the ends of the wires to each end of a D battery. Find a D battery, or a 1.5 volt battery, and move the ends of the wire so that each wire end is touching an end of the battery. You’ll need to use your fingers to hold the ends in place.<ref>https://education.jlab.org/qa/electromagnet.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 5.jpg|center]]
#*One wire end should be at the negative end of the battery while the other wire end should be at the positive end of the battery.
#*Use your thumb to hold one end together and your pointer finger to hold the other end together.

#Hold the wires to the battery’s ends and test the electrical current. Once you have a good grip on the battery with the wires, test it out! Hold the battery and iron close to a small metal object, such as a paperclip or safety pin. If the nail, screw, or bolt picks up the metal object, the magnet is working.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX9QBwJBI_Y</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 6.jpg|center]]
#*If the battery becomes hot, use a small towel to hold the wires to the battery.
===Increasing the Magnet's Power===

#Use a power pack instead of a single battery. Power packs last longer and create a stronger electric current than a single battery. They're available at hardware stores and battery shops, and you can use them just as you would a normal battery.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 13.jpg|center]]

#Find a larger piece of metal. Instead of using a nail, try using a longer metal rod that's about {{convert|1|ft|cm|abbr=on}} long. Be sure to use it with a power pack to create a stronger magnet. It'll take a lot more copper wire to go around the entire piece of metal, so make sure you start with a full spindle.<ref>https://sciencing.com/make-super-strong-permanent-magnets-6520830.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 14.jpg|center]]
#*Wrap the wire tightly around the metal so that the electrical current conducts well.

#Add more wraps of copper wire around the metal. The more coils you create, the stronger the electric current. Get a large spindle of wire and make as many wraps as you can to create a very powerful magnet, adding several layers of wire on top of one another, if desired.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 15.jpg|center]]
*Place a small piece of masking tape over each end of the wire when it's attached to the battery to keep it in place, if desired.
*Never use high voltage electricity with a large amount of current, as it can electrocute you.
*Don't try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage and giving it a large current, which can produce a shock.
*Iron screw, bolt, or nail
*Insulated copper wire
*D-cell battery
*Wire cutters
*Sandpaper or razor
*Metal objects (safety pins, paper clips, etc.)

removed: Magnetic fields are produced when all the electrons in a metal object are spinning in the same direction, either as a natural phenomenon, in an artificially created magnet, or when they are induced to do so by an electromagnetic field.  This article will explain the steps required to produce an electromagnetic field around a steel rod, creating an electromagnet, using simple things which you can find around your home or purchase at the hardware store.
===Make a Simple Electromagnet===

#Get [[Make a Magnet | magnet]] supplies. To make an electromagnet, an electric current is run through a piece of metal, which creates a magnetic field. To make a simple electromagnet, then, you'll need a source of electricity, a conductor, and metal. Look around the house or check out the hardware store to get the following supplies:[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 1.jpg|center]]
#*A large iron nail
#*{{convert|3|ft|m|1}} of thin coated copper wire
#*A D-cell battery
#*Small magnetic objects, like paperclips or pins
#*Wire strippers
#*Masking tape
#*Small bowl made of plastic or wood

# Strip insulation from the ends of the wire.  In order for the wire to effectively conduct electricity, its ends must be stripped of their protective insulation. The stripped ends will be wrapped around the two ends of the battery. Use the wire strippers to remove a few centimeters of insulation from either end of the copper wire. [[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 2.jpg|center]]

#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 3.jpg|center]]

#Wrap the nail. Grasp the wire about {{convert|8|in|cm|1}} from the end. Position it at the head of the nail and wrap it around the nail. Make a second wrap adjacent to the first one; it should touch the first wrap, but not overlap it. Continue wrapping the nail until you've covered it all the way to the tip.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 4.jpg|center]]

#*It's essential to wrap the nail with the wire always running in the same direction, so that the electricity can flow in one direction. If you wrap the wire in different directions, the electricity will flow in different directions, and you won't create a magnetic field.

#Connect the wire ends to the battery. Wrap the exposed end of one side of the wire around the metal part of the battery on the positive side. Wrap the other exposed end to the negative side of the battery. Place a small piece of masking tape over the wrapped wire on both sides to keep it in place.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 5.jpg|center]]

#*The side of the battery you attach the wire to will determine the polarity of the magnetic field you are creating. Switching the wires will also switch the poles. Either way, the nail will become magnetized.
#*When you attach the second wire end, the battery will begin conducting electricity through the wire coil immediately. The nail will grow hot, so be careful not to burn yourself.

#Test the magnet. Once the wires are attached to the battery and the electricity starts flowing, the nail will become magnetized. Test it by placing it against a paperclip or another small piece of metal. If the nail picks up the metal object, the magnet is working.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 6.jpg|center]]
===Add a Switch===

#Cut two pieces of wire. Instead of using just one piece of wire, you'll need two pieces: one should be about {{convert|6|in|cm|1}} long, the other about {{convert|2|yd|m|1}}. Strip all four wire ends back about {{convert|1|in|cm|adj=on|1}}.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 7.jpg|center]]

#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 8.jpg|center]]

#Wrap the nail with the longer piece of wire. Starting about {{convert|8|in|cm|1}} from the end of the wire, wrap the nail from the head to the end with tight coils that touch, but do not overlap. Continue wrapping until the entire nail is covered.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 9.jpg|center]]

#Attach wire to the battery. Attach one end of the wire wrapped around the nail to the positive end of the battery. Attach one end of the smaller piece of wire around the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Attach the mechanical switch.<ref>http://www.energizer.com/learning-center/science-center/Pages/make-electromagnet.aspx</ref> You can use a regular mechanical switch or a knife switch to make this electromagnet, both available for purchase at hardware stores. If you don't want to buy a switch, make your own by following these instructions:[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 11.jpg|center]]
#*Get a small block of wood, two thumbtacks, and a paperclip.
#*Tack the end of the copper wire wrapped around the nail to the block of wood by wrapping it around the metal part of a thumbtack and pushing it into the wood.
#*Wrap the end of the short wire leading from the battery around the other tack. Use the tack to fasten the paperclip to the wood about {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} from the first tack.

#Use the switch. To make the electric current flow, turn the switch on. If you're using a homemade switch, slide the paperclip toward the first tack until it touches the tack. This will complete the circuit and cause the current to flow. To switch off the current, swivel the paperclip away from the first tack.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 12.jpg|center]]
===Increase the Magnet's Power===

#Use a power pack instead of a single battery. Power packs last longer and create a stronger electric current than a single battery. They're available at hardware stores and battery shops.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 13.jpg|center]]
#Use a larger piece of metal. Instead of using a nail, try using a longer metal rod. Be sure to use it with a power back to create a stronger magnet.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 14.jpg|center]]

#Make more wraps around the metal. The more coils you create, the stronger the electric current. Adding a new coil is like adding another magnet. Get more wire and make as many wraps as you can to create a very powerful magnet.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 15.jpg|center]]
*Remember, more wire means more power.
*If the magnet does '''not''' work, see if there are any breaks in your circuit, the only way this project works is that there has to be some sort of current running through the objects.
*This requires '''low voltage''' electricity. '''Never''' use high voltage electricity with a large amount of current, as it can electrocute you.
*Always do the loops. Without loops you have no resistance, causing the battery to heat up too much. Be '''extremely''' cautious!
*Don't '''ever''' try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage and giving it a large current, which means a shock for anything that touches it.
*Don't leave the wires connected to the battery too long because you will use up all of the energy in the battery.
*A lantern battery or a '''D''' cell flashlight battery
*A screw or a nail
*Copper wire
*Wire Stripper
*Vinyl electrical tape or masking tape
*Mechanical switch

== Steps ==
===Make a Simple Electromagnet===

#Get [[Make a Magnet | magnet]] supplies. To make an electromagnet, an electric current is run through a piece of metal, which creates a magnetic field. To make a simple electromagnet, then, you'll need a source of electricity, a conductor, and metal. Look around the house or check out the hardware store to get the following supplies:[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 1.jpg|center]]
#*A large iron nail
#*{{convert|3|ft|m|1}} of thin coated copper wire
#*A D-cell battery
#*Small magnetic objects, like paperclips or pins
#*Wire strippers
#*Masking tape
#*Small bowl made of plastic or wood

# Strip insulation from the ends of the wire.  In order for the wire to effectively conduct electricity, its ends must be stripped of their protective insulation. The stripped ends will be wrapped around the two ends of the battery. Use the wire strippers to remove a few centimeters of insulation from either end of the copper wire. [[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 2.jpg|center]]

#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 3.jpg|center]]

#Wrap the nail. Grasp the wire about {{convert|8|in|cm|1}} from the end. Position it at the head of the nail and wrap it around the nail. Make a second wrap adjacent to the first one; it should touch the first wrap, but not overlap it. Continue wrapping the nail until you've covered it all the way to the tip.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 4.jpg|center]]

#*It's essential to wrap the nail with the wire always running in the same direction, so that the electricity can flow in one direction. If you wrap the wire in different directions, the electricity will flow in different directions, and you won't create a magnetic field.

#Connect the wire ends to the battery. Wrap the exposed end of one side of the wire around the metal part of the battery on the positive side. Wrap the other exposed end to the negative side of the battery. Place a small piece of masking tape over the wrapped wire on both sides to keep it in place.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 5.jpg|center]]

#*The side of the battery you attach the wire to will determine the polarity of the magnetic field you are creating. Switching the wires will also switch the poles. Either way, the nail will become magnetized.
#*When you attach the second wire end, the battery will begin conducting electricity through the wire coil immediately. The nail will grow hot, so be careful not to burn yourself.

#Test the magnet. Once the wires are attached to the battery and the electricity starts flowing, the nail will become magnetized. Test it by placing it against a paperclip or another small piece of metal. If the nail picks up the metal object, the magnet is working.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 6.jpg|center]]
#*When you're finished using the magnet, detach the wire ends from the battery.
===Add a Switch===

#Cut two pieces of wire. Instead of using just one piece of wire, you'll need two pieces: one should be about {{convert|6|in|cm|1}} long, the other about {{convert|2|yd|m|1}}. Strip all four wire ends back about {{convert|1|in|cm|adj=on|1}}.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 7.jpg|center]]

#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 8.jpg|center]]

#Wrap the nail with the longer piece of wire. Starting about {{convert|8|in|cm|1}} from the end of the wire, wrap the nail from the head to the end with tight coils that touch, but do not overlap. Continue wrapping until the entire nail is covered.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 9.jpg|center]]

#Attach wire to the battery. Attach one end of the wire wrapped around the nail to the positive end of the battery. Attach one end of the smaller piece of wire around the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Attach the mechanical switch.<ref>http://www.energizer.com/learning-center/science-center/Pages/make-electromagnet.aspx</ref> You can use a regular mechanical switch or a knife switch to make this electromagnet, both available for purchase at hardware stores. If you don't want to buy a switch, make your own by following these instructions:[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 11.jpg|center]]
#*Get a small block of wood, two thumbtacks, and a paperclip.
#*Tack the end of the copper wire wrapped around the nail to the block of wood by wrapping it around the metal part of a thumbtack and pushing it into the wood.
#*Wrap the end of the short wire leading from the battery around the other tack. Use the tack to fasten the paperclip to the wood about {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} from the first tack.

#Use the switch. To make the electric current flow, turn the switch on. If you're using a homemade switch, slide the paperclip toward the first tack until it touches the tack. This will complete the circuit and cause the current to flow. To switch off the current, swivel the paperclip away from the first tack.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 12.jpg|center]]
===Increase the Magnet's Power===

#Use a power pack instead of a single battery. Power packs last longer and create a stronger electric current than a single battery. They're available at hardware stores and battery shops.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 13.jpg|center]]
#Use a larger piece of metal. Instead of using a nail, try using a longer metal rod. Be sure to use it with a power back to create a stronger magnet.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 14.jpg|center]]

#Make more wraps around the metal. The more coils you create, the stronger the electric current. Adding a new coil is like adding another magnet. Get more wire and make as many wraps as you can to create a very powerful magnet.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 15.jpg|center]]
== Video ==
{{Video:Make an Electromagnet|}}
== Tips ==
*Remember, more wire means more power.
*If the magnet does '''not''' work, see if there are any breaks in your circuit, the only way this project works is that there has to be some sort of current running through the objects.
== Warnings ==
*This requires '''low voltage''' electricity. '''Never''' use high voltage electricity with a large amount of current, as it can electrocute you.
*Always do the loops. Without loops you have no resistance, causing the battery to heat up too much. Be '''extremely''' cautious!
*Don't '''ever''' try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage and giving it a large current, which means a shock for anything that touches it.
*Don't leave the wires connected the the battery too long because you will use up all of the energy in the battery.
== Things You'll Need ==
*A lantern battery or a '''D''' cell flashlight battery
*A screw or a nail
*Copper wire
*Wire Stripper
*Vinyl electrical tape or masking tape
*Mechanical switch

Look around the house or check out the hardware store to get the following supplies:[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 1.jpg|center]]
#*A large black dildo
#*{{convert|3|ft|m|1}} of thin coated copper wire
#*A Dick
#*Carson's mother
#*Strippers
#*Cocaine
#*Small tits

# Strip insulation from the ends of the wire.  In order for the wire to effectively conduct electricity, its ends must be stripped of their protective insulation. The stripped ends will be wrapped around the two ends of the battery. Use the wire strippers to remove a few centimeters of insulation from either end of the copper wire. [[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 2.jpg|center]]

#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 3.jpg|center]]

#Wrap the nail. Grasp the wire about {{convert|8|in|cm|1}} from the end. Position it at the head of the nail and wrap it around the nail. Make a second wrap adjacent to the first one; it should touch the first wrap, but not overlap it. Continue wrapping the nail until you've covered it all the way to the tip.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 4.jpg|center]]

#*It's essential to wrap the nail with the wire always running in the same direction, so that the electricity can flow in one direction. If you wrap the wire in different directions, the electricity will flow in different directions, and you won't create a magnetic field.

#Connect the wire ends to the battery. Wrap the exposed end of one side of the wire around the metal part of the battery on the positive side. Wrap the other exposed end to the negative side of the battery. Place a small piece of masking tape over the wrapped wire on both sides to keep it in place.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 5.jpg|center]]

#*The side of the battery you attach the wire to will determine the polarity of the magnetic field you are creating. Switching the wires will also switch the poles. Either way, the nail will become magnetized.
#*When you attach the second wire end, the battery will begin conducting electricity through the wire coil immediately. The nail will grow hot, so be careful not to burn yourself.

#Test the magnet. Once the wires are attached to the battery and the electricity starts flowing, the nail will become magnetized. Test it by placing it against a paperclip or another small piece of metal. If the nail picks up the metal object, the magnet is working.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 6.jpg|center]]
#*When you're finished using the magnet, detach the wire ends from the battery.
===Add a Switch===

#Cut two pieces of wire. Instead of using just one piece of wire, you'll need two pieces: one should be about {{convert|6|in|cm|1}} long, the other about {{convert|2|yd|m|1}}. Strip all four wire ends back about {{convert|1|in|cm|adj=on|1}}.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 7.jpg|center]]

#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 8.jpg|center]]

#Wrap the nail with the longer piece of wire. Starting about {{convert|8|in|cm|1}} from the end of the wire, wrap the nail from the head to the end with tight coils that touch, but do not overlap. Continue wrapping until the entire nail is covered.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 9.jpg|center]]

#Attach wire to the battery. Attach one end of the wire wrapped around the nail to the positive end of the battery. Attach one end of the smaller piece of wire around the other side of the battery.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Attach the mechanical switch.<ref>http://www.energizer.com/learning-center/science-center/Pages/make-electromagnet.aspx</ref> You can use a regular mechanical switch or a knife switch to make this electromagnet, both available for purchase at hardware stores. If you don't want to buy a switch, make your own by following these instructions:[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 11.jpg|center]]
#*Get a small block of wood, two thumbtacks, and a paperclip.
#*Tack the end of the copper wire wrapped around the nail to the block of wood by wrapping it around the metal part of a thumbtack and pushing it into the wood.
#*Wrap the end of the short wire leading from the battery around the other tack. Use the tack to fasten the paperclip to the wood about {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} from the first tack.

#Use the switch. To make the electric current flow, turn the switch on. If you're using a homemade switch, slide the paperclip toward the first tack until it touches the tack. This will complete the circuit and cause the current to flow. To switch off the current, swivel the paperclip away from the first tack.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 12.jpg|center]]
===Increase the Magnet's Power===

#Use a power pack instead of a single battery. Power packs last longer and create a stronger electric current than a single battery. They're available at hardware stores and battery shops.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 13.jpg|center]]
#Use a larger piece of metal. Instead of using a nail, try using a longer metal rod. Be sure to use it with a power back to create a stronger magnet.[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 14.jpg|center]]

#Make more wraps around the metal. The more coils you create, the stronger the electric current. Adding a new coil is like adding another magnet. Get more wire and make as many wraps as you can to create a very powerful magnet.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 15.jpg|center]]
== Video ==
{{Video:Make an Electromagnet|}}
== Tips ==
*Remember, more wire means more power.
*If the magnet does '''not''' work, see if there are any breaks in your circuit, the only way this project works is that there has to be some sort of current running through the objects.
== Warnings ==
*This requires '''low voltage''' electricity. '''Never''' use high voltage electricity with a large amount of current, as it can electrocute you.
*Always do the loops. Without loops you have no resistance, causing the battery to heat up too much. Be '''extremely''' cautious!
*Don't '''ever''' try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage and giving it a large current, which means a shock for anything that touches it.
*Don't leave the wires connected the the battery too long because you will use up all of the energy in the battery.
== Things You'll Need ==
*A lantern battery or a '''D''' cell flashlight battery
*A screw or a nail
*Copper wire
*Wire Stripper
*Vinyl electrical tape or masking tape
*Mechanical switch

added: Magnetic fields are produced when all the electrons in a metal object are spinning in the same direction, either as a natural phenomenon, in an artificially created magnet, or when they are induced to do so by an electromagnetic field.  This article will explain the steps required to produce an electromagnetic field around a steel rod, creating an electromagnet, using simple things which you can find around your home or purchase at the hardware store.
[[Category:Science]]
== Steps ==
===Make a Simple Electromagnet===

#Get [[Make a Magnet | magnet]] supplies. To make an electromagnet, an electric current is run through a piece of metal, which creates a magnetic field. To make a simple electromagnet, then, you'll need a source of electricity, a conductor, and metal. Look around the house or check out the hardware store to get the following supplies:

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 1.jpg|center|550px]]
#*A large iron nail
#*3 feet of thin coated copper wire
#*A D-cell battery
#*Small magnetic objects, like paperclips or pins
#*Wire strippers
#*Masking tape
#*Small bowl made of plastic or wood

#Strip insulation from the ends of the wire. In order for the wire to effectively conduct electricity, its ends must be stripped of their protective insulation. The stripped ends will be wrapped around the two ends of the battery. Use the wire strippers to remove a few centimeters of insulation from either end of the copper wire.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 2.jpg|center|550px]]

#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 3.jpg|center|550px]]

#Wrap the nail. Grasp the wire about 8 inches from the end. Position it at the head of the nail and wrap it around the nail. Make a second wrap adjacent to the first one; it should touch the first wrap, but not overlap it. Continue wrapping the nail until you've covered it all the way to the tip.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 4.jpg|center|550px]]

#*It's essential to wrap the nail with the wire always running in the same direction, so that the electricity can flow in one direction. If you wrap the wire in different directions, the electricity will flow in different directions, and you won't create a magnetic field.

#Connect the wire ends to the battery. Wrap the exposed end of one side of the wire around the metal part of the battery on the positive side. Wrap the other exposed end to the negative side of the battery. Place a small piece of masking tape over the wrapped wire on both sides to keep it in place.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 5.jpg|center|550px]]

#*The side of the battery you attach the wire to will determine the polarity of the magnetic field you are creating. Switching the wires will also switch the poles. Either way, the nail will become magnetized.
#*When you attach the second wire end, the battery will begin conducting electricity through the wire coil immediately. The nail will grow hot, so be careful not to burn yourself.

#Test the magnet. Once the wires are attached to the battery and the electricity starts flowing, the nail will become magnetized. Test it by placing it against a paperclip or another small piece of metal. If the nail picks up the metal object, the magnet is working.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 6.jpg|center|550px]]
#*When you're finished using the magnet, detach the wire ends from the battery.
===Add a Switch===

#Cut two pieces of wire. Instead of using just one piece of wire, you'll need two pieces: one should be about 6 inches long, the other about 2 yards. Strip all four wire ends back about 1 inch.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 7.jpg|center|550px]]

#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 8.jpg|center|550px]]

#Wrap the nail with the longer piece of wire. Starting about 8 inches from the end of the wire, wrap the nail from the head to the end with tight coils that touch, but do not overlap. Continue wrapping until the entire nail is covered.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 9.jpg|center|550px]]

#Attach wire to the battery. Attach one end of the wire wrapped around the nail to the positive end of the battery. Attach one end of the smaller piece of wire around the other side of the battery.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 10.jpg|center|550px]]

#Attach the mechanical switch.http://www.energizer.com/learning-center/science-center/Pages/make-electromagnet.aspx You can use a regular mechanical switch or a knife switch to make this electromagnet, both available for purchase at hardware stores. If you don't want to buy a switch, make your own by following these instructions:

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 11.jpg|center|550px]]
#*Get a small block of wood, two thumbtacks, and a paperclip.
#*Tack the end of the copper wire wrapped around the nail to the block of wood by wrapping it around the metal part of a thumbtack and pushing it into the wood.
#*Wrap the end of the short wire leading from the battery around the other tack. Use the tack to fasten the paperclip to the wood about 1/4 inch from the first tack.

#Use the switch. To make the electric current flow, turn the switch on. If you're using a homemade switch, slide the paperclip toward the first tack until it touches the tack. This will complete the circuit and cause the current to flow. To switch off the current, swivel the paperclip away from the first tack.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 12.jpg|center|550px]]
===Increase the Magnet's Power===

#Use a power pack instead of a single battery. Power packs last longer and create a stronger electric current than a single battery. They're available at hardware stores and battery shops.http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 13.jpg|center|550px]]

#Use a larger piece of metal. Instead of using a nail, try using a longer metal rod. Be sure to use it with a power back to create a stronger magnet.

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 14.jpg|center|550px]]

#Make more wraps around the metal. The more coils you create, the stronger the electric current. Adding a new coil is like adding another magnet. Get more wire and make as many wraps as you can to create a very powerful magnet.http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html

[[Image:Make an Electromagnet Step 15.jpg|center|550px]]
== Video ==
{{Video:Make an Electromagnet|}}
== Tips ==
*If the magnet does '''not''' work, see if there are any breaks in your circuit, the only way this project works is that there has to be some sort of current running through the objects.
*Remember, more wire means more power.
== Warnings ==
*This requires '''low voltage''' electricity. '''Never''' use high voltage electricity with a large amount of current, as it can electrocute you.
*Don't '''ever''' try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage and giving it a large current, which means a shock for anything that touches it.
*Don't leave the wires connected the the battery too long because you will use up all of the energy in the battery.
*Always do the loops. Without loops you have no resistance, causing the battery to heat up too much. Be '''extremely''' cautious!
== Things You'll Need ==
*A lantern battery or a '''D''' cell flashlight battery
*A screw or a nail
*Copper wire
*Wire Stripper
*Vinyl electrical tape or masking tape
*Mechanical switch

added: {{nointroimg}}Magnetic fields are produced when all the electrons in a metal object are spinning in the same direction, either as a natural phenomenon, in an artificially created magnet, or when they are induced to do so by an electromagnetic field.  This article will explain the steps required to produce an electromagnetic field around a steel rod, creating an electromagnet, using simple things which you can find around your home or purchase at the hardware store.
[[Category:Science]]
== Steps ==
===Make a Simple Electromagnet===

#Get [[Make a Magnet | magnet]] supplies. To make an electromagnet, an electric current is run through a piece of metal, which creates a magnetic field. To make a simple electromagnet, then, you'll need a source of electricity, a conductor, and metal. Look around the house or check out the hardware store to get the following supplies:
#*A large iron nail
#*3 feet of thin coated copper wire
#*A D-cell battery
#*Small magnetic objects, like paperclips or pins
#*Wire strippers
#*Masking tape
#*Small bowl made of plastic or wood

#Strip insulation from the ends of the wire. In order for the wire to effectively conduct electricity, its ends must be stripped of their protective insulation. The stripped ends will be wrapped around the two ends of the battery. Use the wire strippers to remove a few centimeters of insulation from either end of the copper wire.
#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.

#Wrap the nail. Grasp the wire about 8 inches from the end. Position it at the head of the nail and wrap it around the nail. Make a second wrap adjacent to the first one; it should touch the first wrap, but not overlap it. Continue wrapping the nail until you've covered it all the way to the tip.

#*It's essential to wrap the nail with the wire always running in the same direction, so that the electricity can flow in one direction. If you wrap the wire in different directions, the electricity will flow in different directions, and you won't create a magnetic field.

#Connect the wire ends to the battery. Wrap the exposed end of one side of the wire around the metal part of the battery on the positive side. Wrap the other exposed end to the negative side of the battery. Place a small piece of masking tape over the wrapped wire on both sides to keep it in place.

#*The side of the battery you attach the wire to will determine the polarity of the magnetic field you are creating. Switching the wires will also switch the poles. Either way, the nail will become magnetized.
#*When you attach the second wire end, the battery will begin conducting electricity through the wire coil immediately. The nail will grow hot, so be careful not to burn yourself.

#Test the magnet. Once the wires are attached to the battery and the electricity starts flowing, the nail will become magnetized. Test it by placing it against a paperclip or another small piece of metal. If the nail picks up the metal object, the magnet is working.
#*When you're finished using the magnet, detach the wire ends from the battery.
===Add a Switch===
#Cut two pieces of wire. Instead of using just one piece of wire, you'll need two pieces: one should be about 6 inches long, the other about 2 yards. Strip all four wire ends back about 1 inch.
#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.

#Wrap the nail with the longer piece of wire. Starting about 8 inches from the end of the wire, wrap the nail from the head to the end with tight coils that touch, but do not overlap. Continue wrapping until the entire nail is covered.
#Attach wire to the battery. Attach one end of the wire wrapped around the nail to the positive end of the battery. Attach one end of the smaller piece of wire around the other side of the batter.

#Attach the mechanical switch.<ref>http://www.energizer.com/learning-center/science-center/Pages/make-electromagnet.aspx</ref> You can use a regular mechanical switch or a knife switch to make this electromagnet, both available for purchase at hardware stores. If you don't want to buy a switch, make your own by following these instructions:
#*Get a small block of wood, two thumbtacks, and a paperclip.
#*Tack the end of the copper wire wrapped around the nail to the block of wood by wrapping it around the metal part of a thumbtack and pushing it into the wood.
#*Wrap the end of the short wire leading from the battery around the other tack. Use the tack to fasten the paperclip to the wood about 1/4 inch from the first tack.

#Use the switch. To make the electric current flow, turn the switch on. If you're using a homemade switch, slide the paperclip toward the first tack until it touches the tack. This will complete the circuit and cause the current to flow. To switch off the current, swivel the paperclip away from the first tack.
===Increase the Magnet's Power===

#Use a power pack instead of a single battery. Power packs last longer and create a stronger electric current than a single battery. They're available at hardware stores and battery shops.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>
#Use a larger piece of metal. Instead of using a nail, try using a longer metal rod. Be sure to use it with a power back to create a stronger magnet.

#Make more wraps around the metal. The more coils you create, the stronger the electric current. Adding a new coil is like adding another magnet. Get more wire and make as many wraps as you can to create a very powerful magnet.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>
== Video ==
{{Video:Make an Electromagnet|}}
== Tips ==
*Remember, more wire means more power.
*If the magnet does '''not''' work, see if there are any shorts in your circuit, the only way this project works is that there has to be some sort of current running through the objects.
== Warnings ==
*Don't '''ever''' try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage, which means, a shock.
*This requires '''low voltage''' electricity. '''Never''' use high voltage electricity, it can electrocute you.
*Don't leave the wires connected the the battery too long because you will short it out.
*Always do the loops. Without loops you have no resistance, causing the battery to heat up too much. Be '''extremely''' cautious!!!!!
== Things You'll Need ==
*A lantern battery or a '''D''' cell flashlight battery
*A screw or a nail
*Copper wire
*Wire Stripper
*Vinyl electrical tape or masking tape
*Mechanical switch

The stripped ends will be wrapped around the two ends of the battery. Use the wire strippers to remove a few centimeters of insulation from either end of the copper wire.
#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.

#Wrap the nail. Grasp the wire about 8 inches from the end. Position it at the head of the nail and wrap it around the nail. Make a second wrap adjacent to the first one; it should touch the first wrap, but not overlap it. Continue wrapping the nail until you've covered it all the way to the tip.

#*It's essential to wrap the nail with the wire always running in the same direction, so that the electricity can flow in one direction. If you wrap the wire in different directions, the electricity will flow in different directions, and you won't create a magnetic field.

#Connect the wire ends to the battery. Wrap the exposed end of one side of the wire around the metal part of the battery on the positive side. Wrap the other exposed end to the negative side of the battery. Place a small piece of masking tape over the wrapped wire on both sides to keep it in place.

#*The side of the battery you attach the wire to will determine the polarity of the magnetic field you are creating. Switching the wires will also switch the poles. Either way, the nail will become magnetized.
#*When you attach the second wire end, the battery will begin conducting electricity through the wire coil immediately. The nail will grow hot, so be careful not to burn yourself.

#Test the magnet. Once the wires are attached to the battery and the electricity starts flowing, the nail will become magnetized. Test it by placing it against a paperclip or another small piece of metal. If the nail picks up the metal object, the magnet is working.
#*When you're finished using the magnet, detach the wire ends from the battery.
===Add a Switch===
#Cut two pieces of wire. Instead of using just one piece of wire, you'll need two pieces: one should be about 6 inches long, the other about 2 yards. Strip all four wire ends back about 1 inch.
#Set up your supplies in a small bowl made of plastic or wood. It's a good idea to contain the energy you're working with in a bowl that won't conduct electricity.

#Wrap the nail with the longer piece of wire. Starting about 8 inches from the end of the wire, wrap the nail from the head to the end with tight coils that touch, but do not overlap. Continue wrapping until the entire nail is covered.
#Attach wire to the battery. Attach one end of the wire wrapped around the nail to the positive end of the battery. Attach one end of the smaller piece of wire around the other side of the batter.

#Attach the mechanical switch.<ref>http://www.energizer.com/learning-center/science-center/Pages/make-electromagnet.aspx</ref> You can use a regular mechanical switch or a knife switch to make this electromagnet, both available for purchase at hardware stores. If you don't want to buy a switch, make your own by following these instructions:
#*Get a small block of wood, two thumbtacks, and a paperclip.
#*Tack the end of the copper wire wrapped around the nail to the block of wood by wrapping it around the metal part of a thumbtack and pushing it into the wood.
#*Wrap the end of the short wire leading from the battery around the other tack. Use the tack to fasten the paperclip to the wood about 1/4 inch from the first tack.

#Use the switch. To make the electric current flow, turn the switch on. If you're using a homemade switch, slide the paperclip toward the first tack until it touches the tack. This will complete the circuit and cause the current to flow. To switch off the current, swivel the paperclip away from the first tack.
===Increase the Magnet's Power===

#Use a power pack instead of a single battery. Power packs last longer and create a stronger electric current than a single battery. They're available at hardware stores and battery shops.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>
#Use a larger piece of metal. Instead of using a nail, try using a longer metal rod. Be sure to use it with a power back to create a stronger magnet.

#Make more wraps around the metal. The more coils you create, the stronger the electric current. Adding a new coil is like adding another magnet. Get more wire and make as many wraps as you can to create a very powerful magnet.<ref>http://resources.schoolscience.co.uk/CDA/11-14/physics/copch33pg3.html</ref>

== Tips ==
*Remember, more wire means more power.
*If the magnet does '''not''' work, see if there are any shorts in your circuit, the only way this project works is that there has to be some sort of current running through the objects.
== Warnings ==
*Don't '''ever''' try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage, which means, a shock.
*This requires '''low voltage''' electricity. '''Never''' use high voltage electricity, it can electrocute you.
*Don't leave the wires connected the the battery too long because you will short it out.
*Always do the loops. Without loops you have no resistance, causing the battery to heat up too much. Be '''extremely''' cautious!!!!!

*A lantern battery or a '''D''' cell flashlight battery

*Copper wire

added: [[Image:The Finished Magnet.jpg|thumb|right|251px]]Magnetic fields are produced when all the electrons in a metal object are spinning in the same direction, either as a natural phenomenon, in an artificially created magnet, or when they are induced to do so by an electromagnetic field.  This article will explain the steps required to produce an electromagnetic field around a steel rod, creating an electromagnet, using simple things which you can find around your home.
It is easy and fun!
#  Get a power pack or a D-cell battery. You can get them at most battery shops.

#  Find a large nail or a bolt, or other piece of steel that can be wound with copper wire.  Size is not critical, but a rod about 1/4 inch (6 millimeters) in diameter, 4 to 6 inches (about 10 to 15 centimeters) long is a good size to start with. Galvanized steel will destroy the electromagnets power do not use anything galvanized.

#  Get 10 feet (about 3 meters) of coated wire. Magnet wire, available from some hobby or electronics shops is ideal, but regular speaker wire, some telephone wire removed from its outer jacket, or even residential electrical wire will work.  For this project, a 24 gauge wire is probably the best size.
#Neatly coil several feet of wire around a nail, in even, uniform wraps. The more wraps you  make, the stronger the magnetic fields will be.
#  Strip about 2 centimeters of insulation off each end of the wire. These will be the ''leads'' you attach to your battery.

#Use some vinyl electrical tape to attach the one wire to each end of your battery for a D cell. For a lantern battery connect the wires to the springs. For multiple batteries, you may need to purchase a battery holder with clips for attaching the wires.
#Find something like a paper clip or straight pin that is made out of steel, and hold the electromagnet close to the object, and you should see your electromagnet pick it up.
# Note your metal object should "stick" to your electromagnet as long as the battery is connected to the wires and has a charge left in it.
#  Remove your wires from the battery terminals when you are through experimenting with it, since the circuit will rapidly discharge the battery, potentially causing it to overheat.
*Wrapping around more loops around the nail will make it more magnetic.
*You may want to invest in a mechanical switch to energise and cut the power to your electromagnet.
*For building projects, like a model construction crane or other mechanical assembly, you will need to make sure your wires are long enough and flexible enough to do what you want them to do.
*D cells also work.

*If the magnet does '''not''' work, see if there are any shorts in your circuit, the only way this project works is that there has to be some sort of current running through the objects. You can also use masking tape to fasten the wires onto the terminals.
*Remember, more wire means more power.
*Don't leave the wires connected the the battery too long because you will short it out.
*This requires '''low voltage''' electricity. '''Never''' use high voltage electricity, it can electrocute you.
*Don't '''ever''' try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage, which means, a shock.
*Always do the loops. No loops means no resistance, causing the battery to heat up so much, possibly exploding. Be '''extremely''' cautious!!!!!
*A lantern battery or a '''D''' cell flashlight battery
*A screw or a nail
*10 feet of wire
*Wire Stripper
*Bigger battery means more power
*Vinyl electrical tape

added: == Steps ==
#  Get a D cell battery. You can get them at most battery shops.

#  Find a large nail or a bolt, or other piece of steel that can be wound with copper wire.  Size is not critical, but a rod about 1/4 inch (6 millimeters) in diameter, 4 to 6 inches (about 10 to 15 centimeters) long is a good size to start with. Galvanized steel will destroy the electromagnets power do not use anything galvanized.

#  Get 10 feet (about 3 meters) of coated wire. Magnet wire, available from some hobby or electronics shops is ideal, but regular speaker wire, some telephone wire removed from its outer jacket, or even residential electrical wire will work.  For this project, a 24 gauge wire is probably the best size.
#Neatly coil several feet of wire around a nail, in even, uniform wraps. The more wraps you  make, the stronger the magnetic fields will be.
#  Strip about 2 centimeters of insulation off each end of the wire. These will be the ''leads'' you attach to your battery.

#Use some vinyl electrical tape to attach the one wire to each end of your battery for a D cell. For a lantern battery connect the wires to the springs. For multiple batteries, you may need to purchase a battery holder with clips for attaching the wires.
#Find something like a paper clip or straight pin that is made out of steel, and hold the electromagnet close to the object, and you should see your electromagnet pick it up.
# Note your metal object should "stick" to your electromagnet as long as the battery is connected to the wires and has a charge left in it.
#  Remove your wires from the battery terminals when you are through experimenting with it, since the circuit will rapidly discharge the battery, potentially causing it to overheat.
== Tips ==
*Wrapping around more loops around the nail will make it more electromagnetic.
*You may want to invest in a mechanical switch to energise and cut the power to your electromagnet.
*For building projects, like a model construction crane or other mechanical assembly, you will need to make sure your wires are long enough and flexible enough to do what you want them to do.
*D cells also work.

*If the magnet does '''not''' work, see if there are any shorts in your circuit, the only way this project works is that there has to be some sort of current running through the objects. You can also use masking tape to fasten the wires onto the terminals.
*Remember, more wire means more power.
== Warnings ==
*Don't leave the wires connected the the battery too long because you will short it out.
*This requires '''low voltage''' electricity. '''Never''' use high voltage electricity, it can electrocute you.
*Don't '''ever''' try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage, which means, a shock.
*Always do the loops. No loops means no resistance, causing the battery to heat up so much, possibly exploding. Be '''extremely''' cautious!!!!!
== Things You'll Need ==
*A lantern battery or a '''D''' cell flashlight battery
*A screw or a nail
*10 feet of wire
*Wire Stripper
*Bigger battery means more power
*Vinyl electrical tape
== Related wikiHows ==
*[[Make a Simple Electromagnet|How to Make a Simple Electromagnet]]

*A lantern battery or a '''D''' cell flashlight battery

*Don't leave the wires connected the the battery too long because you will short it out.
*This requires '''low voltage''' electricity. '''Never''' use high voltage electricity, it can electrocute you.
*Don't '''ever''' try to insert the wire into a plug. This will conduct the electricity, making it at a high voltage, which means, a shock.
*Always do the loops. No loops means no resistance, causing the battery to heat up so much, possibly exploding. Be '''extremely''' careful when making the loops.
== Steps ==
#Get a lantern battery. You can get them at most battery shops.

#  Find a large nail or a bolt, or other piece of steel that can be wound with copper wire.  Size is not critical, but a rod about 1/4 inch in diameter, 4 to 6 inches long is a good size to start with.

#  Obtain a length of insulated copper wire.  Magnet wire, available from some hobby or electronics shops is ideal, but regular speaker wire, some telephone wire removed from its outer jacket, or even residential electrical wire will work.  For this project, a 24 gauge wire is probably the best size.
#Neatly coil several feet of wire around a nail, in even, uniform wraps. The more wraps you  make, the stronger the magnetic fields will be.
#Strip about 2 centimeters of insulation off each end of the wire. These will be the ''leads'' you attach to your battery.

#Use some vinyl electrical tape to attach the one wire to each end of your battery for a D cell. For a lantern battery connect the wires to the springs. For multiple batteries, you may need to purchase a battery holder with clips for attaching the wires.
#Find something like a paper clip or straight pin that is made out of steel, and hold the electromagnet close to the object, and you should see your electromagnet pick it up.
# Note  your metal object should "stick" to your electromagnet as long as the battery is connected to the wires and has a charge left in it.
#  Remove your wires from the battery terminals when you are through experimenting with it, since the circuit will rapidly discharge the battery, potentially causing it to overheat.

*Wrapping around more loops around the nail will make it more electromagnetic.

*D cells also work.

== Steps ==
# wind the copper wire around the metal rod until most of it is covered.
#  hook the two batteries together
#  hook the two end of the copper wire to the + and - ends of the two connected batteries
#  put it against something and watch it work
#  unhook wire to stop
== Tips ==
*the more copper wire you use and the bigger the metal bar, the more power you can get.
*try using higher voltages to get real strong pull
== Warnings ==
*do not plug wire into electric socket
== Things You'll Need ==
*Two twelve volt batteries
*Metal rod
*copper wire
